lessons.title: Race preview: {{nextRace}}
lessons.objective: Preview this week's race and understand what {{driver}} needs to do.

payload.prompt: {{nextRace}} is a {{track}} track. What does that tell you about this race?

options.text: A short track means bumper-to-bumper racing and lots of contact.
An intermediate means aero and handling dominate.
A superspeedway means pack racing and the Big One is likely.

explanation.correct: Each track type has its own rhythm. Know the track, know what to expect from the race.
explanation.incorrect: Track type shapes everything: short tracks = contact, intermediates = aero, superspeedways = pack racing. Understanding the track tells you what to watch for.

payload.prompt: {{driver}} has won {{track}} before. What does that mean for Sunday?

facts.label: Driver history
facts.value: Has won here in the past

options.label: He is a threat to win.
options.consequence: Past success at a track is a real advantage. Familiarity with setup, grip and passing lanes matters.
considerations: Drivers who win here know how to manage the surface.

options.label: One win does not mean much.
options.consequence: True that conditions change and cars differ year to year. But past success still signals strength.

payload.expertNote: Track history is a real signal. Drivers who have won at a place usually return with an advantage in setup and racecraft.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: He needs a good qualifying run on Sunday to avoid the traffic.

options.text: Starting position matters for track position and avoiding early trouble.
Qualifying does not affect the race.
The fastest car always comes from the back.

payload.translation: A good starting position sets him up to avoid early chaos and stay in contention.

followUps.line: Does he usually qualify well here?
followUps.why: Shows you are thinking about track-specific trends.

followUps.line: What is his biggest challenge at this track?
followUps.why: Invites her to name a specific weakness or strength.

payload.title: Race week talk
payload.setting: She is excited about this week's race and wants to talk about {{driver}}'s chances.

exchanges.theirMessage: I think {{driver}} has a real shot this week. He has been fast lately.

replies.text: What has he been doing well? Is it his speed, pit crew, or setup?
replies.theirResponse: Good question. His car has felt better the last few weeks.
replies.coachNote: You asked about specifics. That invites deeper talk.

replies.theirResponse: Me too. Do you think the track suits him?
replies.coachNote: Sympathy is kind, but ask about his strengths.

payload.closingNote: Race preview talk is about what to watch for Sunday.

payload.prompt: Most Cup races are {{distance}} miles or less, decided by track length.
payload.template: Most Cup races are {{distance}} miles or less, decided by track length.

explanation.correct: Right. Most Cup races are between 300-500 miles. Shorter tracks have many laps; longer tracks have fewer.
explanation.incorrect: Race distance typically ranges 250-600 miles. Understanding the distance helps you predict pit cycles and fuel strategy.

lessons.title: Last race, explained
lessons.objective: Explain what happened last weekend in plain English.

payload.prompt: Last race, {{driver}} finished {{position}}. What does that mean for his Chase hopes?

options.text: A top-five finish gave him strong race points and stage points.
A mid-pack finish costs him ground in points.
His finish does not affect points at all.

explanation.correct: Finish position determines race and stage points. Every position matters in the Chase.
explanation.incorrect: Your driver's finish last week tells you where he stands in points. Better finishes = more points = better Chase position.

payload.prompt: Last race, the winning strategy was to stay out on old tires late. Was that a great call?

facts.label: Strategy
facts.value: Stayed out under caution; did not pit

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: Other teams pitted for fresh tires

options.label: Yes, smart pit strategy.
options.consequence: Knowing when to stay out and trust your tires is a key skill. Track position often beats rubber.

options.label: Partially luck.
options.consequence: It took guts and faith. The caution timing had to work out. Smart and lucky.

payload.expertNote: Stay-out calls often look brilliant or foolish depending on what happens next. This one worked.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: The pit crew won that race on that four-tire stop.

options.text: A quick pit stop gained track position and set up the finish.
The pit crew has no impact on race results.
Pit stops only matter at superspeedways.

payload.translation: A fast stop can be the difference between a win and a loss. Pit crew matters.

followUps.line: What was the pit stop time?
followUps.why: Shows you are paying attention to the details.

followUps.line: How does his crew's speed compare to the competition?
followUps.why: Starts a conversation about consistent team strength.

payload.prompt: Last race, {{driver}} was 15th with five laps to go and finished 12th. Good drive?

options.label: Solid. He drove well at the end.
options.consequence: Passing is hard, especially late. Gaining three spots shows racecraft and car speed.

options.label: He just finished 12th; not special.
options.consequence: Fair point; 12th is mid-pack. But the late drive shows he had something for others.
considerations: The finish position is what counts.
But the direction he was going matters.

payload.expertNote: How a driver is running at the end tells you about car speed and momentum going into next week.

payload.title: Last race debrief
payload.setting: She wants to talk about what happened at last week's race.

exchanges.theirMessage: That race was wild. I am still mad about the pit call.

replies.text: Which stop cost him? Was it tires, speed, or a penalty?
replies.theirResponse: The first one. He got caught speeding on entry.
replies.coachNote: You asked what went wrong and where. That is the right level.

replies.theirResponse: It really did. We could have won.
replies.coachNote: Sympathy is fine, but dig into the specific pit issue.

exchanges.theirMessage: He recovered to 12th, but we lost like six spots on that stop.

replies.text: Did he make up ground on the track after that, or was the damage too much?
replies.theirResponse: He was faster the last stage, but it was not enough time.
replies.coachNote: You are tracking the pit loss vs the race recovery.

replies.text: Well, at least he did not DNF and stayed on the lead lap.
replies.theirResponse: True, but we should have been way better with the car he had.
replies.coachNote: Silver lining is good, but acknowledge the frustration first.

payload.closingNote: Debrief last week to understand what matters heading into the next race.

lessons.title: Chase picture
lessons.objective: Read the Chase standings and explain where {{driver}} stands.

payload.prompt: In the 2026 Chase, seed 1 (regular-season champ) gets {{points}} points. Seed 16 gets {{points16}}. What is the edge?

options.text: A 100-point head start.
A 25-point head start.
No head start; everyone starts at the same points.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 Chase resets: seed 1 gets 2,100, seed 16 gets 2,000. That 25-point cushion rewards the regular-season champion.
explanation.incorrect: The points reset gives the regular-season leader a 25-point head start. In a 10-race Chase, 25 points can decide the title.

payload.prompt: The Chase is {{races}} races long. The driver with the most points after {{track}} wins the title.
payload.template: The Chase is {{races}} races long. The driver with the most points after {{track}} wins the title.

explanation.correct: Perfect. The 2026 Chase is ten races from Darlington to Homestead. Homestead decides the title.
explanation.incorrect: The Chase is ten races (Darlington through Homestead). Homestead, the final race, determines the champion.

payload.prompt: {{driver}} is 11th in Chase points, 45 points behind the leader with 8 races left. Can he win?

options.label: Yes, one win could put him back in it.
options.consequence: A win (55 points) closes the gap fast. With eight races left, a hot streak is possible.

options.label: Unlikely; 45 points is a big gap.
options.consequence: True that the gap is real. But one win closes it halfway. A win plus strong finishes could work.

payload.expertNote: 45 points in 8 races is tight, but wins and consistency in the Chase have come from worse positions.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: He is not in the Chase yet. He needs to be in the top 16 after Darlington.

options.text: Top 16 in regular-season points makes the Chase; everyone else is out.
All 40 drivers are automatically in the Chase.
Only the top three are invited to the Chase.

payload.translation: The Chase is for the top 16 in points after 26 races. If he is outside that window, he is watching from home.

followUps.line: How many points ahead of 17th is he right now?
followUps.why: Shows you are tracking his cushion above the cutoff.

followUps.line: How many races until the Chase cuts off?
followUps.why: Reminds you that the regular season has a deadline.

lessons.title: {{driver}} this week
lessons.objective: Explain how your driver is performing and what matters for them.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: {{driver}} has been good at intermediates this year. That is why I am hopeful this week.

options.text: Track type performance matters; knowing your driver's strengths helps you predict races.
All drivers perform the same at all tracks.
Track type does not affect racing.

payload.translation: Some drivers excel at certain track types. Knowing your driver's specialty tells you when to be excited.

followUps.line: Which track types are not his strength?
followUps.why: Invites you to think about his weaknesses too.

followUps.line: Why do you think he is good at intermediates?
followUps.why: Starts a conversation about handling, setup, or racecraft.

payload.prompt: {{driver}} is 8th in points but has had bad luck the last three races. Should you expect a rebound?

facts.label: Team status
facts.value: No major changes to car or crew

options.label: Yes, he was running well before.
options.consequence: Bad luck breaks. If the car was fast and the crew was sharp before, return to form is likely.

options.label: Three straight races means he is struggling.
options.consequence: Fair concern. But context matters. Were the issues driver errors, mechanical, or just bad luck?

payload.expertNote: A driver's trend before a bad stretch often predicts the rebound. Consistency over luck.

payload.prompt: {{driver}} is known for strong {{strength}}. What advantage does that give him this season?

options.text: Restart jumps mean he wins positions on restarts, which helps in races with many cautions.
Road-course racecraft means he excels on road courses and can beat oval specialists there.
Short-track experience means he handles contact and tire management better than most.

explanation.correct: Every driver archetype has times when their specialty shines. Knowing your driver's edge helps you predict his best weekends.
explanation.incorrect: Driver types each have their specialty. Restart specialists shine in caution-heavy races; road-course ringers own road courses; short-track aces thrive on bumpy ovals.

payload.title: Talk about {{driver}}
payload.setting: She wants to talk about her driver's prospects and what he needs to do.

exchanges.theirMessage: {{driver}} has been solid, but he is not in the conversation for the title yet.

replies.text: How far back is he from the leader? Can he make up ground with six races left?
replies.theirResponse: About 60 points. Possible, but he needs to be perfect.
replies.coachNote: You asked about the gap and the math. That is real championship talk.

replies.text: Yeah, he is too far back.
replies.theirResponse: I think so. But one good race can change things.
replies.coachNote: Agree with her reasoning, then ask about the upside.

exchanges.theirMessage: The next three races are supposed to suit him.

replies.text: What do you mean by suit him? Is it track type, or his car's strength?
replies.theirResponse: Both. He loves short tracks and the car is quick there.
replies.coachNote: You asked her to explain her reasoning. That deepens the conversation.

replies.theirResponse: Right? Do you think he can win any of them?
replies.coachNote: Enthusiasm is good, but ask her to make a prediction based on track fit.

payload.closingNote: Knowing your driver's strengths tells you which weeks to be most hopeful.

lessons.title: Why are fans talking about this?
lessons.objective: Understand the current storyline everyone is discussing.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: Everyone is talking about that pit call. I think it was wrong.

options.text: A controversial pit call divides the fanbase; smart to ask what she means before agreeing.
Pit calls are never controversial.
Everyone always agrees on strategy decisions.

payload.translation: When a high-stakes call goes wrong, fans debate it. Join the conversation without pretending you know more than you do.

followUps.line: What would you have done instead?
followUps.why: Invites her to explain her own reasoning, which often deepens her investment.

followUps.line: Did it change who won, or was the outcome already set?
followUps.why: Asks her to think about how much the call mattered.

payload.prompt: This week a driver complained the rules are unfair. Is that a real issue or just talk?

options.text: Real. Rule changes do happen based on driver and fan feedback.
Just talk. Rules never change.
It depends on who is complaining.

explanation.correct: Driver voices do shape rules. Sometimes it takes a big name to be heard. Sometimes it takes a groundswell of fan opinion.
explanation.incorrect: Rules change based on feedback from drivers, teams and fans. Knowing who has influence in the conversation helps you understand the politics.

payload.prompt: Half the fanbase loves the new rule; half hates it. Who is right?

options.label: Both can be right.
options.consequence: Rule debates rarely have a right answer. One side values fairness; the other values racing quality. Both are real.

options.label: One side is obviously right.
options.consequence: You might lean one way, but the debate is legitimate. The sport will keep evolving.
considerations: There is no objective truth here.

payload.expertNote: Racing rule debates are never settled. The sport always trades off action, fairness, tradition and innovation.

payload.title: Debate talk
payload.setting: There is a hot debate about something in racing, and she wants to know what you think.

exchanges.theirMessage: That new rule is going to ruin the sport. Everyone is mad.

replies.text: Why do you think it is bad? What is wrong with it?
replies.theirResponse: It takes away strategy. Now it is just chaos.
replies.coachNote: You asked her to explain instead of agreeing. That keeps the talk real.
You agreed too fast. Ask her to explain her view first.

exchanges.theirMessage: But some fans think it makes racing better.

replies.text: What do you think they mean? How could it be better?
replies.theirResponse: More passing, I guess. More action.
replies.coachNote: You named both sides of the debate. That is real conversation.

replies.text: So there is real people on both sides of this?
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, half the fans want action; half want tradition.
replies.coachNote: Acknowledging both sides shows balance, even if you lean one way.

payload.closingNote: Learn to hold both sides of a debate; NASCAR fans are divided on most big questions.

lessons.title: What to say Monday
lessons.objective: Prepare to talk about the race and what it means.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: Did you see the race? {{driver}} was {{position}} again.

options.text: A good opening is to name what you saw about his race, then ask a follow-up about strategy or the day.
You should always lie and say you watched if you did not.
You should change the subject to something else.

payload.translation: Start with what happened in the race. A simple observation opens the door to real conversation.

followUps.line: Was that a good day for him, or tough luck?
followUps.why: Invites her to say whether the result was deserved.

followUps.line: What did you think of the pit calls?
followUps.why: Moves to strategy, which fans love to discuss.

payload.prompt: {{driver}} had a bad race. Your person is upset. What is the right move?

options.text: Tell her it is just one race and not to worry.
Listen to her feelings and ask what made it tough.
Change the subject to something happier.

explanation.correct: Right. When she is upset, she needs to vent. Listen first; the big-picture perspective comes later.
explanation.incorrect: Reading the room means matching her mood. If she is frustrated, frustration is valid. Let her talk about what went wrong.

payload.prompt: {{driver}} lost the race by half a car length on the last lap. How do you talk about it Monday?

facts.label: Team morale
facts.value: Heartbroken but the car was fast

options.label: Say how close it was and how well he drove.
options.consequence: Validate the effort and the pain. Second place stings more when you nearly won.

options.label: Look on the bright side; he was fast.
options.consequence: True, but timing matters. Let the sadness breathe first, then the silver lining.

payload.expertNote: The best Monday conversations honor the disappointment first, then find the good in it.

payload.prompt: A good Monday line is: '{{verb}} the {{focus}}. Did {{question}}?'
payload.template: A good Monday line is: '{{verb}} the {{focus}}. Did {{question}}?'

explanation.correct: Perfect. A specific observation ('I watched the final lap') plus a question ('Did that look close?') starts real conversation.
explanation.incorrect: Good Monday lines name what you saw, then ask what she thinks. Specific beats vague.

payload.title: Monday after a big race
payload.setting: The race just ended yesterday. It was huge and she is still processing. You both watched.

exchanges.theirMessage: That finish was insane. I can not believe how close it was.

replies.text: Yeah. Do you think he had the car to win, or did the leader just out-drive him at the end?
replies.theirResponse: He had it. That last pit stop put us behind.
replies.coachNote: You asked her to evaluate the speed vs the luck/strategy. That is the right question.

replies.theirResponse: I know, right? I am so mad.
replies.coachNote: Sympathy is good, but ask for her reasoning to go deeper.

exchanges.theirMessage: But at least we are fast going into the Chase.

replies.text: Right. Does he have the speed to make a real run at the title from where he is in points?
replies.theirResponse: I think so. The last few weeks have been solid.
replies.coachNote: You moved from last week to the bigger picture. That is forward-looking talk.

replies.text: Yeah, the season is still young.
replies.theirResponse: True. But we need more wins.
replies.coachNote: Acknowledge the bigger picture, but get specific about what he needs.

payload.closingNote: Monday conversations honor the emotion of Sunday, then look ahead to next week.
